title: Unbounded chat input and streaming output permit resource exhaustion
description: The chat streaming API accepts an arbitrarily large messages array and forwards it without any client-side length, token, count, or content-size limit. It also accumulates every parsed response chunk in an in-memory array and waits indefinitely for completion, with no timeout, maximum response size, or cancellation path. A caller can submit oversized chat histories or keep a stream open while generating unbounded output, consuming browser memory and potentially imposing unbounded LLM/API usage on the backend.

trace.description: The exported streamMessages method receives caller-controlled messages; its caller is outside this file, and the parameter has no size or element-count restriction.
The complete messages value is forwarded directly to the chat endpoint, with no client-side token, byte, or request-count limit.
Each response chunk is retained in the chunks array, allowing memory use to grow with the response rather than being bounded by a maximum output size.

The generator continues waiting until the stream signals completion and has no timeout, maximum duration, maximum chunk count, or cancellation handling, so a stream that never completes can retain the subscription and buffered data indefinitely.

title: Malformed or split SSE data can hang the chat stream
description: Streaming response data is treated as JSON without exception handling. Any malformed or incomplete SSE data reaching this client causes JSON.parse to throw from the subscription callback. In particular, the implementation does not retain an incomplete final line between download-progress events, so a JSON record split across progress boundaries can be parsed prematurely. The normal error path is bypassed, while done remains false and the async generator can remain pending indefinitely, creating a client-side availability and resource-retention failure.

trace.description: streamMessages is the client-facing entry point for streamed data returned by the chat service; the upstream response source is outside this file.
Download progress text is divided into lines independently for each progress event, without preserving a partial line for the next event.

Each data record is parsed directly as JSON without try/catch or validation. A malformed record or a valid record split across progress events can throw before the subscription's error handler marks the stream done.

title: Caller-controlled basket ID used for cross-user basket mutations
description: The service accepts a caller-controlled target basket identifier and uses it to read and mutate basket data without performing any ownership or authorization check in this file. `mergeGuestBasketIntoUserBasket` calls `find(targetBasketId)`, then creates or updates basket items using the supplied basket context. If the backend endpoints do not independently enforce that the authenticated user owns the basket, a user can substitute another user's basket ID and add items to or alter that basket (BOLA).

trace.description: `mergeGuestBasketIntoUserBasket` is an exported service method; its caller is outside this file and supplies `targetBasketId` without an ownership context or server-derived basket identity.
The supplied basket ID is used to retrieve the target basket, with no ownership check visible before the response is consumed.
The target basket's products are used to derive existing basket-item IDs, which are then selected for mutation based only on the returned data and caller-selected basket.

A new basket item is posted with `BasketId: targetBasketId`, allowing the caller-controlled identifier to become a persisted object property; the client performs no authorization or allow-list enforcement for this property.

title: Guest basket is deleted even when merge requests fail
description: The merge workflow treats failed item writes as successful completion and clears the guest basket unconditionally. Every `put`/`save` request converts errors to `of(null)`, after which the `tap` callback removes the local guest basket regardless of whether any item was persisted. A transient backend failure, invalid target basket, authorization rejection, or partial failure can therefore silently discard guest basket contents and create an inconsistent merge state.

trace.description: `mergeGuestBasketIntoUserBasket` is invoked by a caller outside this file with a target basket ID and begins a state-changing merge workflow.
The service constructs one or more write requests for guest-basket products, and each request converts errors into a successful observable value via `catchError(() => of(null))`.
`forkJoin` completes after those error-swallowed requests, so partial or total write failure is not propagated as a merge failure.
The `tap` callback clears the guest basket unconditionally after the observable completes, deleting source data even when writes returned `null` because of errors.

title: Unbounded guest-basket size and merge request fan-out
description: Guest basket contents are accepted and persisted without a meaningful maximum item count or quantity cap. The caller-controlled quantity is accumulated and written to session storage, and the merge later creates one network request per distinct stored product. A caller can fill the guest basket up to the browser storage limit and trigger a large batch of HTTP requests during merge, consuming client memory, network connections, and backend request capacity. This is primarily a low-severity client/server resource-consumption risk and may be mitigated by infrastructure or backend limits not visible here.

trace.description: `addToGuestBasket` is callable by code outside this file and accepts a caller-controlled quantity without an upper bound or item-count limit.
The quantity is accumulated into an existing item or appended as a new item, with no maximum enforced before storage.
The complete guest basket is serialized into session storage without an application-level size or count limit.

During merge, each distinct guest product becomes a separate HTTP write request and all requests are executed together through `forkJoin`, allowing a large stored basket to generate a large request burst.

title: Unbounded local backup file parsing can exhaust browser resources
description: The restore operation accepts a caller-supplied File and reads and parses it without any size limit. `File.text()` materializes the entire file in browser memory, and `JSON.parse()` then processes the complete contents synchronously. A user who can persuade a victim to select a very large or computationally expensive JSON file can cause excessive memory consumption, UI freezing, tab termination, or browser instability. No file-size check or bounded parsing occurs before these operations.

trace.description: The caller outside this file supplies an arbitrary local `File` to the exported `restore` method.
The entire attacker- or user-selected file is read into memory with `backupFile.text()` and passed into a promise callback without a size limit.
The complete file contents are synchronously deserialized with `JSON.parse`, creating an unbounded memory and CPU consumption sink.

title: Unsanitized feedback comment passed through bypassSecurityTrustHtml
description: Feedback comments received from the feedback service are embedded directly into an HTML string and then passed through Angular's security bypass API. Because the comment is not sanitized before being marked as trusted HTML, attacker-controlled feedback content can inject HTML such as an event-handler payload (for example, an element with an onerror handler). The trusted value is then supplied to the gallery as the feedback caption content, where it can be rendered into the DOM, resulting in stored or reflected client-side XSS depending on feedback persistence and exposure.

Each feedback comment is interpolated into an HTML fragment containing a figcaption and paragraph. No validation or context-appropriate sanitization is applied to the comment before interpolation.
The constructed HTML, including the untrusted comment, is explicitly marked trusted with bypassSecurityTrustHtml, disabling Angular's normal HTML sanitization.
The trusted HTML value is passed as gallery image arguments for rendering as feedback content, providing the path to the DOM HTML-rendering sink.

title: Password change sends credentials in a GET URL
description: The password-change operation is tested as a GET request with the current and new passwords embedded directly in the URL query string. URL data is commonly retained in browser history and may be recorded by reverse proxies, web servers, monitoring systems, and Referer headers. An attacker who gains access to those records could recover the user's current or replacement password. Password-changing operations should use an authenticated POST/PUT request with credentials in the protected request body and should avoid placing secrets in URLs.

trace.description: The test invokes UserService.changePassword with the current password and replacement password supplied as request data.

The expected request URL includes current=foo, new=bar, and repeat=bar as query parameters, establishing that the service places password values in the URL rather than keeping them in a protected request body.
The test requires the request to use GET, so the password-bearing URL is sent as the password-change operation's HTTP request.

title: OAuth access token exposed in request URL
description: The OAuth access token is passed as an access_token query parameter in a GET request to Google's user-info endpoint. Query-string tokens can leak through browser history, intermediary/proxy logs, URL telemetry, and Referer propagation. Anyone obtaining such a token may be able to retrieve the associated user's OAuth profile data or use the token until it expires or is revoked. The token should be transmitted using the provider's supported authorization-header mechanism where possible.

trace.description: The test invokes UserService.oauthLogin with an OAuth access token supplied by the caller.
The expected outbound URL appends the caller-supplied token as access_token=at in the query string.
The test confirms that the token-bearing request is issued as a GET request to the external Google user-info endpoint.

title: Raw API errors are logged directly to the browser console
description: The accounting component's error paths are explicitly tested to write raw API error values directly to the browser console. The test covers product, order, quantity, delivery-status, and update failures, including logging an entire error object. Browser console output is visible to the end user and can expose backend diagnostics, identifiers, or other response details; it also bypasses centralized security logging and monitoring. The production logging implementation is outside this file, but this test establishes and preserves the behavior as expected.

The component's product-loading error path is exercised after receiving the failed API response.
The test requires the error to be emitted through console.log, codifying direct browser-console exposure of the raw API error.

title: Client-controlled price and inventory values lack robust validation
description: The accounting component sends caller/UI-supplied identifiers and monetary or inventory values directly to mutation services without enforcing business bounds or validating type/format. `modifyQuantity` only clamps negative values to zero, while `modifyPrice` does the same; neither rejects NaN, Infinity, excessively large values, or other invalid numeric representations. If the corresponding API trusts these client-provided values, an attacker can invoke the component methods or reproduce the requests to corrupt inventory or product pricing.

The supplied quantity is transformed only with a negative-value check and is then placed into the request body; there is no finite-number, maximum, or format validation.
The supplied price is likewise only clamped when negative and is then sent to the product mutation service without robust validation.
The service calls perform the inventory and product-price mutations using the untrusted identifier and value. Server-side validation is not visible in this file.

title: Accounting view loads unbounded collections before client-side pagination
description: The component fetches the complete product catalog, complete inventory collection, and complete order history before applying pagination only in the browser. The calls use empty-search or `getAll()` operations and no page, limit, or result-size bound is supplied. If these APIs return unbounded collections, a single authenticated visit or repeated reload can force the client and API to allocate and transfer the entire dataset, creating a denial-of-service or degraded-service condition as the data grows.

Product loading requests an empty search, which is an unbounded catalog query from this component, and stores the complete response in memory before configuring the paginator.
Order loading calls `getAll()` and stores every returned order in `orderData`; the paginator is configured only after the full response has been received and materialized.

title: Address API errors are intentionally logged directly to the browser console
description: The test suite explicitly requires address-loading and address-deletion failures to be written directly to the browser console. If the propagated error contains backend details, identifiers, or other sensitive information, this exposes it to any script or user with browser access and provides no structured security logging or monitoring. The concrete error value in this file is only the literal string `Error`, and the actual logging implementation is outside this file, so exploitability and sensitivity are not fully confirmable here.

title: Address deletion forwards caller-supplied ID without an ownership check
description: The component exposes a deletion method that accepts an address identifier from its caller and forwards it directly to the address service. No ownership, authorization, or validation check is performed in this component before initiating deletion. If the backing service/API does not independently scope the deletion to the authenticated user, an attacker can invoke this handler with another user's address ID and trigger a BOLA/unauthorized deletion. The caller and server-side authorization logic are outside this file, so exploitability cannot be confirmed here.

The supplied identifier is forwarded unchanged to `AddressService.del(id)` without a local ownership, authorization, or allow-list check.

`addressService.del(id)` initiates the address deletion operation. If the service/API trusts the identifier without server-side user scoping, substituting another user's ID enables unauthorized deletion.

title: Potential IDOR/BOLA in address edit workflow
description: The edit workflow trusts an attacker-controlled route parameter as the address identifier. A caller can navigate to an arbitrary `addressId`; the component retrieves that address and later submits an update for the same identifier without any ownership or authorization check in this code. If the corresponding backend service does not independently scope the lookup and update to the authenticated user, User A can read and modify User B's address by substituting User B's ID in the route.

On save, the same unverified identifier is passed to `AddressService.put`; this is the mutation sink that can overwrite another user's address if the backend does not enforce ownership.

title: Repeated saves accumulate route subscriptions and amplify address lookups
description: `ngOnInit()` subscribes to `ActivatedRoute.paramMap`, but successful saves call `ngOnInit()` directly instead of reusing or disposing the existing subscription. Each successful save therefore creates another long-lived subscription. When route parameters subsequently emit, every accumulated subscription invokes `getById`, multiplying network requests and retaining subscription state. Repeated edits can cause increasing client-side memory use and request amplification, degrading the client and potentially the address API.

After a successful edit, the component manually invokes `ngOnInit`, adding another subscription while the previous one remains active.
Each accumulated subscription can call `getById` on a later route-parameter emission, causing unbounded request amplification and retained subscription resources.

title: Stored XSS through trusted feedback HTML
description: Feedback content received from the backend is explicitly marked as trusted HTML without sanitization. A user who can submit feedback containing HTML such as an event-handler payload can cause that content to be rendered as active markup in the administration UI when the feedback table or details view binds it as HTML. This creates stored client-side XSS against administrators or other users viewing feedback.

title: Stored XSS through trusted user email HTML
description: User email values returned by the backend are interpolated into an HTML string and explicitly marked as trusted HTML. If an attacker can control or influence an email value, the resulting markup can execute when the administration UI renders the trusted value, producing stored client-side XSS in an administrative context.

The component iterates over the externally supplied user records and embeds each user.email value into an HTML string without an input-specific sanitization step.

title: Privileged password policy is advisory and bypassable
description: The component attempts to enforce a stronger password policy for privileged support accounts only in client-side code, and the only response to a violation is a console message. The password-change request is still submitted unconditionally with the supplied new password. An attacker can bypass this control by invoking the change-password flow directly, disabling JavaScript, modifying localStorage, or simply ignoring the browser-side warning; the server must enforce the privileged-account policy because this client check does not prevent the operation.

The privileged-account determination is based on attacker-modifiable client-side localStorage, and a failed complexity check only emits a console message; no control flow prevents submission.
The component submits the current, new, and repeated passwords to UserService regardless of whether the privileged-account check failed.

title: Raw password-change errors exposed through client console logging
description: Failed password-change responses are written wholesale to the browser console. The component does not restrict the fields or format of the error object, so any server-provided diagnostic details, internal error information, or other sensitive response data can be exposed to anyone able to inspect the user's browser console. This is also not a reliable security audit trail for password-change failures because client-side console output is local and can be cleared or suppressed.

The asynchronous response has a dedicated error path for rejected password changes.
The complete error object is emitted with console.log before being assigned to component state, exposing whatever diagnostic fields the response contains in the browser console.

title: Sensitive account routes lack authentication and resource-access guards
description: Several account- and transaction-sensitive client routes are registered without any authentication or authorization guard. `saved-payment-methods`, `order-completion/:id`, and `order-history` are directly navigable, while the `privacy-security` parent and its `data-export` child are also unguarded. The `:id` route additionally accepts a caller-controlled order identifier without any route-level ownership check. Angular route guards are not a substitute for server-side authorization, but omitting even the client-side access-control boundary exposes these workflows to unauthenticated users and makes accidental reliance on component/API checks more likely. An attacker can navigate directly to paths such as `/order-history`, `/order-completion/<other-order-id>`, or `/privacy-security/data-export`; backend enforcement is not visible in this file and must be independently verified.

The `order-completion/:id` route accepts a caller-controlled order identifier and is also registered without a guard, so navigation can target an arbitrary identifier before any component-level or API authorization is known to occur.
The `order-history` route is directly reachable without `LoginGuard`, unlike nearby address routes that explicitly require login.
The `privacy-security` parent route has no guard; its child routes therefore do not inherit an authentication boundary from this configuration.
The `data-export` security-sensitive child route is exposed under the unguarded parent and has no own `canActivate` guard, providing a concrete unguarded endpoint in the client workflow.

title: Password-change policy permits weak five-character passwords
description: The password-change form is explicitly tested as valid for a new password meeting only a five-character minimum (the test title states a 5–40 character policy, and the control accepts values such as the short password used here). If this client-side policy is relied upon by the password-change workflow, an attacker can select a highly guessable five-character password, substantially weakening account protection. The server-side policy cannot be confirmed from this file, so the finding is limited to the insecure design encoded and enforced by the component's form contract.

The test asserts that the short-policy password is valid, establishing the weak acceptance boundary for the password-change workflow.

title: Unbounded challenge notification queue enables client-side resource exhaustion
description: The component appends a notification for every accepted socket event but never imposes a maximum queue length, expiry, or backpressure. An attacker or malfunctioning upstream capable of causing repeated `challenge solved` events can grow `notifications` without bound, retaining attacker-influenced message, flag, and country data and repeatedly triggering change detection. This can consume browser memory and degrade or crash the client.

For every non-hidden event, the component forwards the received data to `showNotification` without rate limiting or quantity checks.
`showNotification` pushes each event into the persistent `notifications` array, with no maximum size or eviction policy, and then triggers change detection.

title: Socket listener is never removed when the component is destroyed
description: The component registers a socket listener during `ngOnInit`, but this file contains no corresponding `ngOnDestroy` cleanup or listener removal. If the component is instantiated more than once during application navigation or testing, each instance remains subscribed, causing every subsequent socket event to invoke multiple callbacks and potentially multiple network requests, notification insertions, and confetti imports. Repeated component creation can therefore amplify resource use and create a client-side denial-of-service condition.

`ngOnInit` registers a persistent `challenge solved` listener on the socket, but no teardown callback is registered alongside it.
The registered callback remains able to process future events and invoke notification handling, progress persistence, and other work after the component instance should have been discarded.

title: Continue code is persisted without explicit cookie security attributes
description: A server-returned value named `continueCode` is stored in a long-lived browser cookie using only an expiration option. The code does not request Secure or SameSite protections, and a cookie created by client-side JavaScript is inherently script-readable rather than HttpOnly. If `continueCode` is a bearer-like progress or authorization token, exposure through non-transport-restricted cookies increases the impact of any browser compromise and permits transmission over an unintended non-HTTPS request. The one-year lifetime further extends the exposure window.

The returned value is treated as a credential-like continuation value and retained for one year.
The value is written to the `continueCode` cookie with only `expires` configured; no Secure or SameSite options are supplied, and client-side cookie creation cannot provide HttpOnly.

title: Unbounded and automatically triggered LLM requests from URL input
description: The component accepts an arbitrarily long `initialMessage` from the URL query string and automatically submits it without user confirmation or a length limit. A crafted link can therefore cause a victim's browser to initiate an LLM request merely by loading the conversation route. The same path also permits attacker-controlled content to be submitted directly through `sendMessage`. This can consume LLM/API quota and cause resource use without an intentional user action. The request/stream path has no visible input-size, timeout, cancellation, or response-size cap; streamed output is appended indefinitely to the in-memory message and then persisted, allowing excessive memory, storage, token, and provider consumption.

Any non-empty query value is automatically passed to `sendMessage` during component initialization, without a confirmation gesture or abuse-prevention check. A victim visiting a crafted conversation URL triggers the request.
`sendMessage` accepts the content and adds it to the conversation, while constructing the complete conversation history for submission. There is no per-message or total-history size limit.

The unbounded conversation history is submitted to the chat service and consumed through an async stream. No timeout, cancellation, maximum number of chunks, maximum output length, or rate limit is enforced in this component.

The `for await` loop continues until the service ends the stream, and every `deltaContent` is concatenated into the in-memory message. An oversized or non-terminating provider response can grow memory and subsequent persisted storage without a local cap.

title: Unbounded challenge content causes client-side resource consumption
description: The component accepts externally supplied challenge fixes and source code without any size or count limits. `shuffle()` copies every supplied fix, allocates a random sort key for each item, and performs an O(n log n) sort; the selected fix and original snippet are then loaded into CodeMirror. If challenge content can be influenced by an attacker or served from an untrusted backend, an oversized fixes array or very large code strings can consume substantial browser CPU and memory, causing the coding-challenge page to become unresponsive. No bounding or truncation control is visible in this file.

title: Upload restrictions are enforced only in the client
description: The component relies on browser-side file restrictions before sending attacker-controlled files to the upload endpoint. `allowedMimeType` and `maxFileSize` are enforced by `ng2-file-upload` in the client and can be bypassed by submitting a direct request to `/file-upload`. The selected file is then uploaded with no server-side validation visible in this file. If the endpoint does not independently enforce size and content limits, an attacker can submit oversized or unexpected archive/XML/YAML content, potentially causing excessive memory, CPU, disk, or parser resource consumption. The server-side handler is outside this file, so the existence of backend enforcement cannot be confirmed here.

The selected file is uploaded directly to the configured `/file-upload` endpoint. A caller can bypass the UI and client-side filters by issuing the request independently; server-side size, type, and safe-content validation are not shown in this file.

title: Unsanitized data export rendered with document.write
description: The export response's `userData` is written directly into a newly opened browser document. The value originates from the data-export API and is not sanitized or constrained before reaching `document.write`. If exported data contains attacker-controlled fields (for example, a malicious value stored in a user's profile or other exported record), the resulting HTML can execute script in the newly opened window, leading to client-side XSS. The same operation is an injection sink because attacker-controlled data is interpreted as HTML rather than rendered as text.

title: Security sanitizer bypass applied to CAPTCHA HTML
description: The component explicitly disables Angular's HTML sanitization for the `image` field returned by the CAPTCHA service. No sanitization or allowlist is applied before the value is trusted as HTML. If the CAPTCHA endpoint or its response can be influenced by an attacker, arbitrary HTML supplied in `data.image` can be rendered through the component's template and execute as client-side XSS. The exploitability of the source is not fully confirmable from this file because the template and service implementation are outside the target.

title: Client-controlled UserId is submitted as the feedback owner
description: The component sends a caller-controlled `UserId` as part of the feedback object. Although the value is initially populated from `whoAmI`, `userIdControl` is a client-side form control and can be modified by an attacker through browser developer tools or a scripted invocation before `save()` runs. `save()` then overwrites the feedback object's `UserId` with that client-controlled value and submits it. If the feedback API uses this field to associate the feedback with a user without deriving the identity from the authenticated session, User A can submit feedback attributed to User B, or potentially manipulate another user's feedback ownership. The server-side endpoint is outside this file, so whether it performs an ownership check cannot be confirmed here.

title: Service errors are exposed through direct browser-console logging
description: The test suite explicitly codifies that errors returned by both the address and delivery services are written directly to the browser console. description: The password-recovery UI triggers a security-question lookup after a one-second client-side delay, but there is no server-enforced rate-limit or request cancellation visible here. description: The reset form accepts a new password with only a five-character minimum in this component. title: Untrusted product descriptions bypass Angular HTML sanitization
description: Product descriptions returned by `ProductService.search` are explicitly converted into trusted HTML without a visible sanitization or allowlist step. Product data can be attacker-influenced through product-management functionality elsewhere in the application; once a malicious description is returned, this component disables Angular's protection and passes it to the template for HTML rendering. A payload such as an event-handler-bearing element in a product description could execute when users view search results.

trace.description: `ngAfterViewInit` receives product records from the external `ProductService.search` response; the service and attacker-facing product-data entrypoint are outside this file.
The returned product array is passed to `trustProductDescription`, including each product's dynamic `description` field.

Each description is marked as trusted HTML via `bypassSecurityTrustHtml` without a visible sanitization or restrictive allowlist, disabling Angular's XSS protection before the value is rendered by the component template.

title: Raw restore errors exposed through browser console logging
description: The component logs raw error objects from challenge-progress restoration directly to the browser console. These errors may contain backend response bodies, internal endpoint details, stack traces, or other diagnostic data. Because browser-console output is visible to the affected user and is not sanitized or reduced to a safe error identifier, an attacker who can trigger a failed restore operation can inspect potentially sensitive implementation details. The same unsafe logging pattern occurs for all three restore flows.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file: a socket 'server started' event invokes the callback, causing client-side progress restoration and its error handlers to run.
A failed restoreProgress request supplies its raw error object to the callback; equivalent raw error paths exist for restoreProgressFindIt and restoreProgressFixIt at lines 71 and 80.
The raw error object is written to console.log without redaction or normalization. Equivalent sinks occur at lines 72 and 81, exposing backend error details through the browser console.

title: Untrusted product and search content is explicitly trusted as HTML
description: The test verifies that attacker-influenced product descriptions are passed directly to Angular's `bypassSecurityTrustHtml` API. The test input contains an executable script payload, and the assertion requires the bypass API to receive it without requiring sanitization. If the component renders the resulting trusted value, stored or API-supplied product content can execute arbitrary JavaScript in users' browsers. The analogous search-query test also requires URL query data containing a script tag to be trusted as HTML.

trace.description: The test receives attacker-controlled product data from the mocked product search response; the caller/API supplying this data is outside this file.
The component is exercised with the malicious product description and the fixture is rendered, establishing the data path into the component's rendering behavior.
The test stubs the sanitizer's security bypass method rather than requiring safe sanitization, so the bypass result cannot provide a meaningful security guarantee.
The assertion explicitly requires the untrusted script payload to reach `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, an HTML-trust sink. A separate test does the same for a query-parameter payload at lines 218-221.

title: Authentication status is based only on presence of an arbitrary localStorage token
description: The test defines successful authentication as the mere presence of any value in browser localStorage: the arbitrary string `abc` is accepted as proof that the user is logged in. This is not cryptographic token validation and is forgeable by client-side code or an attacker who gains same-origin script execution. If this result controls access to privileged UI or actions, it creates a client-side authentication bypass; server-side authorization must not rely on this check.

trace.description: The test invokes the component's authentication helper, whose implementation is outside this file.
The test places the arbitrary, unsigned, unexpired value `abc` in localStorage and treats its presence as sufficient authentication state.
The assertion confirms that any present localStorage value is accepted as logged-in state, with no signature, expiration, issuer, or server verification represented by the tested behavior.

title: Authentication bearer token stored in localStorage
description: The component treats a bearer authentication token stored in browser localStorage as the client-side login state. The token is read directly from localStorage and remains available to any JavaScript executing in the origin, including an injected or compromised third-party script. Such a script can retrieve the token and replay it against authenticated API endpoints. Removing the token during logout does not mitigate theft before logout, and this file does not show a stronger HttpOnly, Secure cookie-based session mechanism.

trace.description: Angular invokes ngOnInit as the component is initialized; the caller/framework entrypoint is outside this file.
The component checks browser localStorage for the authentication token and uses its presence to decide whether to load authenticated user details.

The token is directly retrieved from localStorage as the authentication state, making it readable by same-origin JavaScript and therefore vulnerable to theft if an XSS or compromised script executes in the application origin.

title: Client-side role check based on decoded token payload
description: The accounting-role decision is made in the client by decoding the token payload and comparing the embedded role to the accounting role. If tokenDecode only decodes rather than cryptographically verifies the token, a user can modify or forge the payload and cause accounting-only navigation or controls to be shown. Even if tokenDecode verifies the signature, this client-side check must not be relied upon as authorization because the component provides no server-side enforcement for the resulting decision. The actual template/caller and protected operation are outside this file, so exploitability of a privileged action cannot be confirmed here.

trace.description: The component is initialized by the Angular framework, and its template or other caller is outside this file; that external code can invoke the role-dependent isAccounting decision.
The component obtains a token payload through loginGuard.tokenDecode(), but this file does not demonstrate signature verification or server-derived role validation.

Access to the accounting condition is determined solely by the decoded payload's role field. A forged or tampered client token can satisfy this check unless tokenDecode performs verified signature validation, and client-side visibility is not a substitute for server-side authorization.

title: Authentication token persisted in JavaScript-readable local storage
description: The component is explicitly expected to persist the authentication token in browser local storage. Any same-origin JavaScript executing in the application context can read `localStorage.getItem('token')`, enabling token theft and session takeover after an XSS or compromised third-party script. The test also verifies cookie persistence, but this file does not establish whether that cookie is configured with secure, `SameSite`, or HttpOnly protections. The local-storage persistence alone is a concrete insecure authentication/session-storage design.

trace.description: The caller and production authentication flow are outside this test file; this test supplies a successful 2FA response containing an authentication token.
The test invokes the component's 2FA verification workflow, causing the supplied token to be processed by the component.

The test asserts that the authentication token is written to browser local storage under the `token` key, making it readable by any same-origin script and therefore directly useful for session-token theft.

title: Security test mocks HTML sanitizer as an identity function and approves attacker-shaped HTML
description: The test configures DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml to return its input unchanged, then explicitly verifies that an HTML-bearing order ID is accepted as trusted HTML. This weakens the security control in the test fixture and codifies unsafe behavior rather than asserting that attacker-controlled order IDs are escaped or rejected. The test itself is not attacker-facing, but it can allow a production client-side XSS regression to pass unnoticed if the component renders this trusted value through an HTML binding. The corresponding production caller and DOM binding are outside this file.

trace.description: The test assigns an HTML payload to the component's orderId input; in production, the caller that supplies this value is outside this file.
The mocked order service returns the same orderId value to the component, exercising the path that processes the order identifier.
The component is initialized with the HTML-bearing order identifier, causing its order-ID rendering logic to execute.

The test double replaces DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml with an implementation that returns the supplied HTML unchanged, so no sanitization or escaping occurs before the value is treated as trusted.

title: Wallet backend errors are logged only to the browser console
description: The test explicitly verifies that an error returned by the wallet backend is written directly to the browser console. If the production component passes through backend error objects, those errors may contain internal implementation details or other sensitive diagnostic data, while the event is not sent to an application logging/monitoring system. This can expose details to the client and leaves wallet-service failures difficult to detect centrally. The finding is limited-confidence because the actual logging implementation is outside this specification file and the test uses only a generic error string.

trace.description: The test configures the wallet service mock to return an error value; the caller and production error source are outside this file.
The component's balance-loading workflow is invoked after the mocked backend failure is configured.

The test verifies that the returned error is written directly via console.log, indicating client-only logging rather than centralized security-relevant monitoring and potentially exposing backend diagnostic content to browser users.

title: Wallet address is sent as an identity without signature-based ownership verification
description: The component treats a wallet address returned by the injected-wallet connector as an authenticated identity and sends it to the backend without obtaining a cryptographic signature or challenge response. A wallet connection establishes account availability, but does not prove to the backend that the caller controls the address. If the walletAddressSend endpoint uses this value to authenticate, register, mint, or authorize actions, an attacker can bypass ownership verification by submitting another user's address directly to that endpoint. The server must verify a signed, domain-bound challenge and reject reused or expired challenges.

trace.description: Angular invokes the component lifecycle hook from outside this file; the hook begins wallet authentication handling.
The component connects to the injected wallet and receives the selected account from the connector.
The connector-provided account is copied into metamaskAddress and becomes the identity used by subsequent application logic.

The address is sent to the backend through walletAddressSend, but this file performs no challenge creation, signature request, signature verification, nonce validation, or other proof-of-control step before the identity-bearing request.

title: Remote Solidity compiler artifact is consumed without integrity verification
description: The component accepts Solidity source from its external caller and sends it to a compiler whose JavaScript artifact URL is constructed from a fixed filename but is not accompanied by an application-level checksum, signature, or other integrity verification. A compromise of the Solidity binary distribution origin, or substitution of the downloaded compiler artifact, could cause the browser to execute malicious compiler code or produce attacker-controlled bytecode that is subsequently trusted by this component for deployment. The finding is limited to the integrity boundary visible in this file; the implementation of solidityCompiler is outside the file.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies arbitrary Solidity source through the exported compileAndFetchContracts(code) method.
The selected compiler release is converted into a remote HTTPS URL, while the submitted source is placed into the compiler input. No digest, signature, or pinned artifact content is specified.

The remote compiler is invoked with the URL and untrusted source. The compiler library's fetching and execution behavior is outside this file, but this call provides no visible integrity verification control.

Compiler output is accepted and stored as compiledContracts, later serving as the bytecode and ABI source for deployment. A compromised compiler artifact can therefore influence code executed in the browser or bytecode deployed through the user's wallet.

title: Unbounded client-side Solidity compilation permits resource exhaustion
description: Arbitrary editor content reaches the Solidity compiler without a source-size limit, compilation timeout, or other resource budget. A sufficiently large or computationally pathological Solidity program can consume substantial browser CPU and memory, freeze the tab, or exhaust available resources when a user triggers compilation. This is primarily a client-side denial of service and is dependent on the external caller being able to cause or induce compilation.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and passes editor-controlled Solidity source to compileAndFetchContracts(code).
The supplied source is copied directly into compilerInput.contractBody with no length, complexity, or compilation-budget check.
The component invokes the compiler for the unbounded source and provides no timeout, cancellation, or worker isolation in this code path.
solidityCompiler processes attacker-influenced input in the browser; oversized or pathological input can monopolize client CPU/memory and make the application tab unavailable.

title: Plaintext user password embedded in frontend source
description: Jim's plaintext password, `ncc-1701`, is embedded in the client-side challenge code as the value passed to `waitForInputToNotHaveValueAndNotBeEmpty`. Because this file is part of the frontend, the credential can be recovered by anyone who downloads or inspects the application's JavaScript/source. An attacker can then attempt direct authentication as Jim, bypassing the need for the intended SQL injection challenge and potentially gaining access to Jim's account and data.

trace.description: The exported `LoginJimInstruction` object is frontend-delivered challenge configuration; its caller and the mechanism serving this code are outside this file.
The challenge directs the user to enter an arbitrary non-empty password, while explicitly treating `ncc-1701` as the known password value. This places the credential in a client-side execution path.

The plaintext password `ncc-1701` is embedded directly in the helper call and is therefore recoverable from the frontend source or bundled JavaScript. Using the recovered value against the login flow can authenticate as Jim.

title: Bender login password hardcoded in frontend challenge code
description: The exported challenge instruction embeds Bender's real login credentials in frontend source: the email address is specified at line 78 and the password is present as a literal at line 84. Because this code is shipped to and executed by the browser, a user can inspect the source or compiled bundle and recover the password, then authenticate directly as Bender without performing the intended SQL injection. The password is used as a client-side comparison value, but that still exposes a credential to every frontend user.

trace.description: The exported LoginBenderInstruction object is consumed by a caller outside this file, causing the browser-facing challenge configuration to be loaded and exposed to frontend users.
The instruction explicitly places Bender's email address into the login email field, making the target account identifier part of the client-delivered challenge logic.

The password-field helper contains the literal Bender password as an argument. This secret is therefore embedded in source or the generated frontend bundle and can be recovered by inspecting client assets.

title: Bootstrap errors exposed through client-side console logging
description: If Angular application bootstrap rejects, the caught Error object is written directly to the browser console. Browser-console output is accessible to the user or an attacker controlling a client session and may include stack traces, component/module names, URLs, or other internal diagnostic details. There is no redaction, environment guard, structured telemetry, or centralized handling at this boundary, which can expose internal error information and does not provide reliable security-event monitoring.

trace.description: The application is initialized through Angular's bootstrap promise; failures from this externally triggered application startup flow propagate to the promise returned by bootstrapApplication.
The bootstrap promise is chained with a rejection handler, so any startup error reaches the local catch callback.
The rejection handler logs the complete Error object with console.log without redaction or production-environment filtering, exposing its diagnostic contents in the browser console.

title: Entity decoding after HTML sanitization can reintroduce active markup
description: The notification builder sanitizes the challenge description before entity-decoding it. An attacker-controlled or otherwise untrusted description containing HTML encoded as entities can remain harmless during sanitization and then be converted back into active markup by `entities.decode`. The resulting value is broadcast through Socket.IO; if a client renders the notification as HTML, this can enable client-side HTML/script injection. The client-side rendering and the external caller are outside this file, so exploitability depends on those components.

trace.description: The exported notification function receives a challenge object from a caller outside this file; its `description` field is therefore treated as externally supplied to this function.
The challenge description is passed through `sanitizeHtml` and then entity-decoded. Decoding after sanitization can turn encoded tags or attributes back into active HTML.
The resulting notification, including the decoded description, is emitted to connected Socket.IO clients. Any client that inserts the notification as HTML will interpret the reintroduced markup.

title: Unbounded growth of the in-memory challenge notification cache
description: `sendNotification` unconditionally appends a notification to the process-global `notifications` array, even when an identical challenge key was already present. The `wasPreviouslyShown` check only suppresses the socket emission; it does not prevent the array growth. Because the function is exported and has no deduplication, maximum-size bound, expiry, or eviction, repeated calls—such as repeated restore or externally triggered invocations—can grow memory without limit and eventually degrade or exhaust the process.

trace.description: The exported `sendNotification` function accepts a challenge from a caller outside this file, and callers can invoke it repeatedly for an already-solved challenge.

The code checks whether the challenge key was previously shown, but this result is used only for deciding whether to emit a socket event; it does not prevent another notification from being created and stored.
Every invocation appends to the process-global `notifications` array with no size limit, deduplication, or eviction policy, allowing attacker-influenced repeated calls to consume process memory.

title: Admin status is determined from an unverified JWT claim
description: The admin-login helper treats the `role` claim from a JWT as trusted after only decoding it. `jwtDecode` does not verify the JWT signature, issuer, or expiration, so a caller who can place a token in `localStorage` can forge a payload containing `data.role: "admin"` and cause this helper to report that an administrator is logged in. Any caller that relies on completion of this helper as an authorization gate can therefore be bypassed. Server-side authorization may limit the ultimate impact, but this client-side authentication decision is not trustworthy.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and invokes the exported `waitForAdminLogIn` helper, which is intended to wait until an administrator is considered logged in.
The helper reads the authentication token directly from browser-controlled `localStorage`.
The token is decoded locally with `jwtDecode`; this operation extracts claims but does not cryptographically verify the JWT signature or validate its expiration.

The decoded, attacker-forgeable `payload.data.role` value is accepted as proof of administrator status, and the helper completes when it equals `admin`. This is the authentication/authorization decision sink.

title: Unbounded recursive filesystem scan and full-file buffering
description: The exported filesystem scanner accepts an arbitrary list of paths from its caller and recursively walks every directory while reading each file in full. There is no maximum recursion depth, file count, file size, total bytes, or timeout. A caller that can influence the paths can point the function at a very large directory tree or files with very large contents, causing excessive filesystem I/O and memory use because full file contents are retained in the returned matches array.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller outside this file supplies the `paths` array to the exported `findFilesWithCodeChallenges` function.
The function iterates over every supplied path and recursively invokes itself for directory contents without imposing a depth or item-count limit.
Each directory is fully enumerated and every entry is recursively processed, allowing attacker-influenced paths to expand into arbitrarily large directory trees.
The sink reads each regular file in its entirety and stores the complete content in `matches`; there is no file-size or aggregate-memory limit.

title: Unescaped challenge keys enable regular-expression injection and ReDoS
description: Challenge identifiers are extracted from scanned file content and interpolated directly into regular-expression source. The identifier is not escaped or allow-listed before being used in both `source.match(...)` and `new RegExp(...)`. If a scanned file is attacker-controlled or can be placed under a caller-supplied path, its marker text can inject regex operators, alter matching behavior, trigger invalid-regex exceptions, or cause catastrophic backtracking against large source content. The same path can therefore produce regular-expression injection and CPU exhaustion.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller outside this file supplies paths to the exported scanner, which reads files from those locations.
File contents from the supplied paths become the `file.content` value processed by the challenge parser.
Challenge keys are extracted from file content without restricting their characters or escaping them for regex use.
The untrusted `challengeKey` is interpolated into a string passed to `source.match`, causing it to be interpreted as regular-expression syntax.
The same unescaped key is interpolated into a dynamically constructed `RegExp`, allowing attacker-controlled regex behavior and potentially expensive backtracking during parsing.

title: Unbounded retry and polling configuration permits resource exhaustion
description: The deep-partial configuration validator accepts resource-control values without any positivity, finiteness, or upper-bound checks. In particular, `llmMaxRetries` is accepted as any number, allowing an excessively large value to amplify outbound LLM requests and cause resource exhaustion; similarly, `pollFrequencySeconds` is accepted as any number, including zero or negative values that can cause a tight or continuously failing polling loop if consumed directly. The caller supplying the YAML/configuration is outside this file, but this schema is the validation boundary and establishes no compensating limits.

trace.description: An external caller supplies a possibly incomplete YAML/application configuration to the exported validation schema; the caller is outside this file.
The validator recursively permits partial application sections, including the partially validated chatbot configuration, rather than requiring bounded operational values.
`llmMaxRetries` is validated only as an unconstrained number. No minimum, maximum, or finite-value constraint prevents extreme retry amplification.

title: OAuth authorized redirect targets lack scheme and host restrictions
description: The configuration validation boundary accepts OAuth authorized redirect targets as arbitrary strings. It does not require an absolute URL, restrict schemes such as HTTPS, or enforce an approved host/redirect allowlist. If an attacker can influence a configuration accepted through this validation path, they can add a redirect target under their control; downstream OAuth handling may then redirect authorization results or codes to that target. Whether the downstream OAuth implementation independently enforces an allowlist is not visible in this file.

trace.description: An external caller supplies a possibly incomplete YAML/application configuration to the exported validation schema; the caller is outside this file.
The partial application schema permits the nested Google OAuth configuration and its redirect entries to be supplied from that input.
Each `authorizedRedirects` entry validates `uri` only as `z.string()`, with no URL parsing, HTTPS requirement, or host allowlist.

title: Unvalidated configuration values injected into frontend HTML
description: Application configuration values are inserted directly into the generated frontend HTML without HTML- or URL-context validation. In particular, `application.name` is placed inside a `<title>` element, while cookie-consent fields—including `linkUrl`—are copied into an HTML/JSON-like fragment. If an attacker can influence the deployment configuration (for example through a configuration-management interface, writable environment, or malicious configuration file), they can inject markup or a `javascript:` URL that executes in users' browsers when the frontend is served. The caller and configuration source are outside this file, so exploitability depends on whether those configuration values are attacker-controlled.

trace.description: `customizeApplication` is invoked by a caller outside this file and conditionally processes application configuration values.
The application name is read from configuration and interpolated into a `<title>` element without HTML encoding.

The interpolated title is supplied as the replacement string to a file-rewrite operation that modifies the served `index.html`; an injected closing tag and script/markup would become frontend content.

title: Arbitrary configured URL fetched during application startup
description: The startup customization flow treats a configured URL as a source for a server-side file download. `utils.isUrl` only detects whether the value is a URL; this file applies no domain allow-list, private-network restriction, or resolved-IP validation before calling `utils.downloadToFile`. If an attacker can influence the relevant configuration, the server can be induced to request internal HTTP services such as localhost administration endpoints, private-network services, or cloud metadata endpoints, and write the response into the frontend asset tree. The configuration caller/source is outside this file, so reachability depends on configuration exposure.

trace.description: `customizeApplication` is invoked by a caller outside this file and enables customization based on external application configuration.

`retrieveCustomFile` reads a configured file value and accepts it whenever `utils.isUrl` recognizes it as a URL; no host, scheme beyond URL recognition, network-range, or resolved-address allow-list is present here.
The URL is passed directly to `utils.downloadToFile`, causing the server to make an outbound request to the configuration-selected destination.

title: Hardcoded JWT signing private key enables token forgery
description: The application embeds an RSA private key directly in source code and uses it to sign JWTs. Anyone who obtains this source, build artifact, or leaked repository contents can forge valid RS256 tokens, impersonate users, and potentially satisfy role-based authorization checks.

trace.description: The exported authorize function receives signing requests from callers outside this file and creates authentication tokens.
JWT signing uses the module-level privateKey value, which is hardcoded in the source rather than loaded from a protected secret store.
jwt.sign uses the embedded private key with RS256, so possession of the key permits creation of tokens accepted by the application's public-key verification middleware.

title: Weak unsalted MD5 used for security-sensitive hashing
description: The exported hash helper uses unsalted MD5. If callers use it for passwords, security answers, reset material, or other authentication-related secrets, attackers can use fast brute force and precomputed dictionaries to recover the original values. The helper provides no key stretching or salt.

trace.description: The exported hash function accepts data supplied by callers outside this file, potentially including credentials or security-answer material.
The input is passed directly to crypto.createHash('md5') without a salt, work factor, or password-specific KDF.
The MD5 digest is returned as the final security value, creating a fast and unsuitable password/hash primitive.

title: Hardcoded HMAC secret permits forgery of MAC-protected values
description: The hmac helper hardcodes its HMAC key in source code. Anyone able to read the source or a shipped artifact can compute valid MACs for values protected by this helper, defeating authenticity checks that rely on it.

trace.description: The exported hmac function receives data from callers outside this file and is intended to authenticate or integrity-protect that data.
The function constructs an HMAC using a literal key embedded in the source code.
crypto.createHmac produces the MAC with the exposed literal secret, allowing an attacker with source or artifact access to generate matching MACs.

title: Role authorization accepts expired JWTs
description: The role-checking middleware validates only the JWT signature through jws.verify and then reads the decoded role. jws.verify does not perform JWT claim validation such as expiration checking, so an otherwise valid but expired token can continue to authorize accounting requests. The same verify helper is also used by the deluxe and customer checks.

trace.description: The isAccounting middleware receives an HTTP request from an external route and extracts the bearer token before deciding whether to call next().
The token is checked with the exported verify helper, which delegates to jws.verify rather than jwt.verify and therefore verifies the signature without enforcing exp or other registered claims.
The helper decodes the token and checks only whether data.role equals accounting; no expiration or freshness check occurs between verification and authorization.
A token with a valid signature but an expired exp claim can still reach next() and obtain the accounting-protected operation.

title: Coupons are forgeable because validation lacks authenticity protection
description: Coupon validation checks only that the Z85-decoded value has a current-month format and a two-digit discount. It does not verify a signature or MAC and does not require that the coupon was generated by the server. An attacker can construct a validly formatted current-month coupon with an arbitrary discount, such as 99.

trace.description: The exported discountFromCoupon function receives a coupon from a caller outside this file.
The supplied value is decoded and accepted when its decoded text matches a month-plus-two-digit-discount pattern and the month equals the current month.
The discount is parsed directly from attacker-controlled decoded content; there is no comparison with a server-side signature, MAC, or coupon store.
parseInt returns the attacker-selected discount as an apparently valid coupon result.

title: Substring-based redirect allowlist can be bypassed
description: The redirect allowlist uses substring matching rather than exact URL parsing and comparison. A URL controlled by an external caller can include an allowed URL as a substring while targeting an attacker-controlled host, such as https://evil.example/?next=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop. Any caller that uses this predicate to authorize a redirect can therefore bypass the intended allowlist.

trace.description: The exported isRedirectAllowed function receives a candidate redirect URL from a caller outside this file.
The function iterates through trusted URLs but does not parse the candidate URL or compare its origin and path structurally.
url.includes(allowedUrl) returns true whenever an attacker-controlled URL merely contains a trusted URL as text, allowing an untrusted destination to pass the intended access-control check.

title: Mandatory special memories can bypass required user association
description: The validator accepts a mandatory special memory when its `user` field is absent. The matching condition at line 142 only selects memories where `memory.user` is truthy and different from the required user, so a memory containing the required security-question fields but no associated user bypasses the intended ownership check. This permits an invalid configuration to satisfy the mandatory special-memory validation and can break or subvert workflows that rely on the memory being bound to `john` or `emma`.

trace.description: The caller, outside this file, supplies the `memories` array to the exported configuration validator.
The validator invokes the mandatory special-memory checks for the caller-supplied memories.

The intended user-association check filters only memories with a truthy `memory.user` that differs from the required user. A matching special memory with no `user` value is therefore excluded from the error set and accepted, despite the subsequent error message stating that it must belong to the required user.

title: Unbounded product and memory arrays cause excessive validation work
description: The validator accepts caller-supplied product and memory arrays without any local size limit, then performs multiple full-array scans and allocates filtered result arrays. A caller outside this file that can influence configuration data can provide a very large number of products or memories, causing repeated CPU and memory consumption during startup/configuration validation. No pagination, element-count cap, or other resource bound is enforced in this file.

trace.description: The caller, outside this file, supplies `products` and `memories` to the exported validator; when omitted, they are loaded from configuration without a local size bound.
The validator runs numerous product and memory validation passes sequentially, including minimum-count, uniqueness, special-item, and association checks.

The checks repeatedly traverse the entire arrays and create filtered arrays, for example filtering every memory for each mandatory special-memory definition. With unbounded input sizes, this creates attacker- or operator-controlled CPU and memory work.

title: Unvalidated caller-controlled URL enables server-side request forgery
description: The exported downloadToFile function accepts a URL from its caller and passes it directly to the download library without restricting the destination to an allow-list of trusted hosts, rejecting loopback/private/link-local addresses, or otherwise validating the resolved destination. The caller is outside this file; the architecture includes an unauthenticated profile-image URL upload route that is a plausible attacker-facing caller. An attacker can supply a URL targeting localhost, cloud metadata services, or other internal HTTP services, causing the server to retrieve internal resources. The downloaded response is then written to the supplied destination.

trace.description: The caller outside this file supplies the URL and destination to the exported downloadToFile function; the function accepts the URL without any trusted-host or private-network validation.
The caller-controlled URL is passed directly to download(), with no allow-list, scheme restriction, or resolved-IP validation.
download() performs the outbound request to the attacker-selected destination, enabling access to internal services and metadata endpoints.

title: Unbounded remote download buffers the entire response in memory
description: downloadToFile loads the complete response returned by download(url) into memory before writing it. There is no response-size limit, timeout, streaming-to-disk mode, or other resource bound in this utility. If an attacker can cause an attacker-controlled URL to reach this function (the caller is outside this file and the application exposes an unauthenticated profile-image URL route), the attacker can point it at a large or indefinitely generated response and consume server memory, potentially causing process termination or service degradation.

trace.description: The caller outside this file supplies a URL to the exported downloadToFile function; no maximum download size is enforced at this boundary.
The utility awaits download(url), which returns the full downloaded data rather than writing through a bounded stream.
The full response is held in memory as data and then synchronously written, allowing a large remote response to exhaust process memory.

title: Asynchronous startup precondition failures are not reflected in the success result
description: The precondition routine computes asynchronous checks, including dependency validation, required build files, and port availability, but does not incorporate their result into the returned status. When called with `exitOnFailure: false`, `asyncConditions` may be false while the function still returns `success`, which only reflects the synchronous Node/OS/CPU checks. It also resolves `preconditionsReady` before enforcing the asynchronous result. A caller that relies on the return value or readiness promise can therefore continue startup despite missing required files, unavailable dependencies, or a conflicting port.

trace.description: The exported `validatePreconditions` function receives the `exitOnFailure` option from a caller outside this file; callers can explicitly select the non-exiting path.
The function runs multiple asynchronous prerequisite checks and aggregates their result into `asyncConditions`, including dependency, required-file, and port checks.
The aggregate asynchronous result is only used to decide whether to call `process.exit`; it is not combined into `success` before the function returns.
The function resolves readiness and returns `success`, which can be true even when `asyncConditions` is false if `exitOnFailure` is disabled.

title: Unvalidated URL reaches server-side fetch in domain reachability helper
description: The exported `checkIfDomainReachable` helper accepts an arbitrary URL string and passes it directly to Node's `fetch` without restricting the scheme, hostname, resolved address, or private/link-local ranges. A caller that can supply this argument can make the server perform HTTP(S) requests to localhost, internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, or other attacker-selected destinations. The response body is not returned, making this primarily a blind SSRF/reachability primitive, but the target can still be probed and internal endpoints can be triggered.

The supplied string is used directly as the destination argument to `fetch`; no HTTP(S)-only policy, hostname allowlist, DNS resolution check, or private-network exclusion is applied.
The server initiates the outbound request to the caller-selected destination, providing a blind SSRF and internal network probing capability.

title: Caller-controlled port enables server-side localhost port scanning
description: The exported port-check helper accepts an arbitrary port value and invokes `portscanner.checkPortStatus` against the local host. If reachable from an attacker-controlled caller, this permits probing services bound to the server's loopback/interface ports. There is no port allowlist or authorization/rate control in this helper; the result is exposed through the resolved boolean and warning/info logging.

The supplied value is converted with `parseInt` without an allowlist or restriction to the expected configured application port.
`portscanner.checkPortStatus` performs a server-side connection/status check for the selected port, allowing an externally reachable caller to probe local services.

title: Mass assignment of User.role enables privilege escalation
description: The auto-generated `/api/Users` and `/api/Users/:id` CRUD surface excludes only `password` and `totpSecret`, leaving the sensitive `role` property caller-controlled. A caller can submit `role: "admin"` during user creation or update; the model validates only that the value is one of the supported roles, not that the caller is authorized to assign it. The setter then persists the supplied role, enabling privilege escalation or unauthorized role changes.

The model declares `role` as a persisted user attribute, making it part of the model's creation and update attribute set.
The role field accepts the administrator value and performs only an enum validation; there is no authorization check tying role assignment to a trusted administrator.

The role setter writes the caller-supplied role directly into the persisted User instance. Through the CRUD binding, an attacker can supply `role: "admin"` and obtain or grant administrative privileges.

title: Data erasure bypasses security-answer verification
description: The data-erasure form collects an email address and security answer, but the POST handler never validates either field. It only checks that a session token maps to an authenticated user, then immediately creates a deletion request for that session user. An authenticated attacker can submit any or empty securityAnswer and bypass the intended security-question confirmation, triggering the irreversible privacy workflow without completing the stated verification step.

The handler authenticates only by looking up req.cookies.token in authenticatedUsers. Although it obtains the logged-in identity, it performs no comparison or verification of req.body.securityAnswer or req.body.email.

The handler creates a PrivacyRequest for the authenticated user immediately, with deletionRequested set to true. No security-answer verification or other confirmation check occurs before this destructive workflow is initiated.

title: 2FA setup, disablement, and verification outcomes are not security-audited
description: The 2FA handlers perform security-sensitive authentication-state changes but contain no security-event logging. Failed password/TOTP attempts, successful 2FA setup, and successful 2FA disablement all return responses or update the account without emitting an audit record. An attacker who repeatedly attempts TOTP guesses or disables 2FA after obtaining a user's credentials can therefore do so without application-level records that support detection, investigation, or alerting. A global access log may exist elsewhere, but it would not necessarily capture the security outcome or affected user.

The handler processes the supplied TOTP and returns either an unauthorized response or creates an authenticated session, but neither failed nor successful verification is logged.
The setup handler receives a password, setup token, and initial TOTP token and mutates the user's 2FA state after validation without recording the event or its outcome.

The disable handler receives a password and clears the user's TOTP secret, then returns success without an audit log; the surrounding catch path likewise returns 401 without recording the failed security-sensitive attempt.

title: Broken object-level authorization on basket item updates
description: The PUT basket-item route authorizes only that the caller passed through `security.appendUserId()`. The handler loads the basket item solely by the attacker-controlled `req.params.id`, retrieves the authenticated user, but never compares the item's basket/user ownership to that user. It then calls `next()`, allowing the downstream update handler to mutate the selected item. User A can substitute User B's basket-item ID and change its quantity.

The target object identifier is taken from `req.params.id` and used in a database lookup without scoping the lookup to the authenticated user's basket.
The authenticated user is retrieved but never used for an ownership or authorization comparison.
After checking only that the item exists and optionally validating quantity, the middleware invokes `next()`, handing the unscoped item to the downstream mutation handler.

title: Basket ownership validation can be bypassed when adding items
description: The POST handler's basket ownership check is bypassable. For unauthenticated requests, the condition at line 37 is skipped entirely because it is guarded by `user &&`, even though the route has no authentication middleware beyond `appendUserId()`. Additionally, for an authenticated request, only the first `BasketId` parsed from the raw body is checked, while the last `BasketId` is persisted. An attacker can submit duplicate `BasketId` fields with an acceptable first value and a victim's basket ID as the last value, causing an item to be saved into the victim's basket.

The handler parses attacker-controlled raw request data and collects every `BasketId` occurrence into an array, preserving duplicate fields.
The ownership check is conditional on a user being present and validates only `basketIds[0]`; unauthenticated callers therefore receive no ownership check at all.
The object persisted uses `basketIds[basketIds.length - 1]`, which is not the value validated at `basketIds[0]`.
The attacker-controlled basket ID is saved through `BasketItemModel.save()`, creating a basket item in an unauthorized basket.

title: Negative basket quantities pass stock and limit validation
description: The quantity validation accepts negative quantities. For a negative caller-supplied quantity, the per-user limit comparison (`limitPerUser >= quantity`) and stock comparison (`product.quantity >= quantity`) both normally succeed, so the middleware calls `next()` without rejecting the value. The add handler then persists the raw quantity. This permits invalid basket state and can produce business-logic or pricing corruption wherever basket quantities are later summed.
