The caller-controlled quantity is passed directly into `quantityCheck()` without a nonnegative or integer validation.
The business rules compare the product limit and stock against the supplied quantity, but neither condition rejects negative values.
A negative quantity satisfies `product.quantity >= quantity`, causing validation to call `next()` rather than reject the request.
The subsequent add handler places the unvalidated quantity into the basket-item model and persists it.

title: Unauthenticated exposure of internal application metrics
description: The unauthenticated GET /metrics endpoint directly returns the Prometheus registry. The registry contains internal application and business metrics, including total wallet balance, registered-user counts, order/review/feedback/complaint counts, challenge-solving and cheating metrics. Because the handler performs no authentication or authorization check, any remote caller can repeatedly retrieve these internal operational and business statistics. This is an exposure of internal metrics and a missing access-control boundary.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported handler is registered as unauthenticated GET /metrics and accepts the external request without an authorization check.
The metrics registry includes a total wallet-balance metric, which is populated from the aggregate balance of all users.
The background update loop populates additional internal metrics from orders, reviews, users, wallets, feedback, and complaints, including total balance and user counts.
The handler serializes and ends the complete Prometheus registry in the HTTP response, exposing those metrics to the unauthenticated caller.

title: Unbounded Prometheus label cardinality from attacker-controlled MIME types
description: The file-upload metrics use the attacker-controlled multipart file MIME type as a Prometheus label value. The middleware runs on unauthenticated upload routes, and the value is used without an allow-list or bounded cardinality. An attacker can submit many uploads with distinct arbitrary Content-Type/MIME values; prom-client creates and retains a separate labeled time series for each value, causing unbounded in-process metric memory growth and potentially degrading or exhausting the service.

The middleware reads the request's uploaded file object and proceeds whenever a file exists; no MIME-type allow-list or cardinality limit is enforced here.

The file MIME type is taken directly from the upload metadata and passed as the file_type label value. Upload error paths also reach this callback, so rejected uploads can still create new label values.
prom-client's labeled Counter retains a distinct time series for each distinct label value, allowing repeated unauthenticated uploads with unique MIME types to grow metric state without a bound.

title: User-controlled UserId permits cross-account memory export
description: The data export handler authenticates the bearer token but uses the caller-controlled `req.body.UserId` to select memories. There is no ownership comparison between the authenticated user's ID and this value in the handler. If `security.appendUserId()` does not unconditionally overwrite the request field with the authenticated user's ID, User A can submit User B's `UserId` and receive User B's memories in the export. The route's middleware is outside this file, so its exact overwrite behavior cannot be confirmed here.

The handler authenticates the bearer token and obtains the current user, but this check does not bind the later memory lookup to that user's ID.
The request body field `UserId` is used directly as the memory ownership criterion. No per-resource ownership check against `loggedInUser.data.id` occurs in this handler.
The selected memories are serialized into the export returned to the caller.

title: Unbounded data export enables excessive database and memory consumption
description: The authenticated export endpoint performs three unbounded data reads: all memories for the selected user, all matching orders, and all matching reviews. The results are mapped into arrays and serialized as one JSON string, with no pagination, record limit, response-size cap, timeout, or per-user rate limit visible in this file. An attacker with a valid account can repeatedly invoke the endpoint, or accumulate a large dataset under the account, forcing database work and application memory/serialization costs.

The handler issues an unbounded memory query followed by unbounded order and review queries, with no pagination or maximum-result controls.
Orders and reviews are also fetched without limits, so a single export can materialize arbitrarily many records before response construction.
All fetched records are copied into `userData` and serialized into a single response, creating memory and CPU pressure proportional to the total dataset size.

title: Data exports lack event-specific audit logging
description: Data export is a security-relevant event involving potentially sensitive personal data, but this handler contains no audit logging for successful exports, failed export attempts, or the identity and scope of the export. If application-wide request auditing does not cover this route, repeated bulk exports and abuse would not be attributable or readily detectable from this code path.

The handler performs multiple sensitive data retrievals and handles authentication failures, but no security-event logger is invoked on either the success or failure paths.
The export assembles usernames, email addresses, orders, reviews, and memory metadata into a response without recording an audit event containing the actor, timestamp, or export scope.

title: Unauthenticated ZIP upload permits path traversal file writes
description: The unauthenticated `POST /file-upload` path accepts ZIP archives and writes archive entries to disk using a flawed traversal check. `absolutePath.includes(path.resolve('.'))` does not verify that the resolved path remains inside `uploads/complaints`; for example, an entry such as `../../config/target` resolves under the application directory, still contains the current-working-directory string, and is then written using the unnormalized traversal path. An anonymous attacker can therefore overwrite files reachable by the application, subject to the target directory existing. This is an unsafe file-handling/integrity failure and the dangerous write operation is reachable without authorization.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller outside this file registers this exported handler for unauthenticated `POST /file-upload`; the handler receives the attacker-supplied uploaded file.
The handler accepts files whose attacker-controlled original filename ends in `.zip` and, when the file-write challenge is enabled, passes the attacker-controlled in-memory archive to extraction.

Each archive entry's path is combined with the upload directory and resolved, but the code only performs a substring test against the current working directory rather than enforcing directory containment. Traversal entries such as `../../config/target` can pass this test.
The entry is written using the raw traversal-containing path, allowing an archive entry to escape `uploads/complaints` and overwrite an application-reachable file.

title: Unbounded ZIP upload and extraction enable resource exhaustion
description: The upload-size middleware is effectively a no-op: `checkUploadSize` performs no check and always calls `next()`. The route's preceding `uploadToMemory.single('file')` middleware therefore buffers attacker-controlled request data before any application-level limit, and ZIP processing additionally opens the entire buffer and streams every archive entry without entry-count, expanded-size, or compression-ratio limits. An attacker can submit a very large upload or a decompression bomb to consume memory, CPU, and disk, potentially degrading or exhausting the service.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller outside this file invokes this exported upload-size middleware on the unauthenticated `POST /file-upload` route after the multipart middleware has already produced an in-memory `file` object.
The supposed size check contains no limit, rejection, or accounting and unconditionally forwards the request.
ZIP uploads are passed into extraction whenever the file-write challenge is enabled, with no archive size, entry count, expanded-size, or compression-ratio guard.
The entire attacker-controlled buffer is parsed as an archive and all entries are iterated, allowing large archives or decompression bombs to consume substantial memory and processing resources.

title: Unbounded YAML upload permits memory and CPU exhaustion
description: YAML uploads also pass through the no-op `checkUploadSize` middleware. The handler then parses attacker-controlled YAML and serializes the resulting object inside a VM. Although execution has a two-second timeout, that timeout does not impose a size or memory bound on the upload, YAML object construction, or `JSON.stringify`; a sufficiently large or structurally expensive YAML document can cause high memory and CPU consumption.

`checkUploadSize` does not inspect the file size and always continues, so the YAML handler receives an unbounded attacker-controlled buffer.
For YAML extensions, the raw upload buffer is converted to a string and supplied as `data` to the parsing expression.
`yaml.load(data)` followed by `JSON.stringify(...)` performs potentially expensive parsing and serialization without a size or resource bound; the VM timeout alone does not prevent memory exhaustion.

title: Unauthenticated checkout of arbitrary baskets (BOLA)
description: The checkout endpoint accepts a caller-supplied basket identifier but does not require authentication or verify that the basket belongs to the current user. It loads any basket by primary key and then clears its items and returns an order confirmation. An attacker can submit another user's basket ID to check out and destroy that basket, potentially causing unauthorized orders, inventory changes, and data loss.

The target basket identifier is taken directly from the request path.
The basket is looked up solely by the supplied ID, with no user ownership predicate.
The authenticated user, if any, is only used to derive an email; there is no authentication requirement or comparison between the user and basket owner.
The handler destroys all basket items for the supplied basket ID and returns an order confirmation, allowing the caller to mutate another user's basket after substituting its ID.

title: Caller-controlled UserId enables unauthorized wallet debits and credits
description: The handler trusts req.body.UserId for wallet operations. The caller can choose the user whose wallet is charged and credited, while the route has no authentication or authorization middleware. By supplying a victim's UserId and paymentId=wallet, an attacker can cause the victim's wallet to pay for the attacker's selected basket; the same field also controls where bonus points are credited.

The request body supplies UserId and payment-related order details, with no server-derived user identity used for these wallet operations.
When the caller selects wallet payment, the handler loads the wallet using the caller-controlled UserId and checks its balance.
The handler decrements the selected user's wallet without verifying that the authenticated customer owns that UserId or that the basket belongs to that user.
The same untrusted UserId controls the wallet receiving the order's bonus points, demonstrating that a sensitive model property is bound directly from the request.

title: Forged client-side coupon data grants campaign discounts
description: The checkout logic accepts a base64-encoded couponData value from the request and treats its decoded code and date as sufficient proof of campaign eligibility. Base64 provides no authenticity or integrity protection. Anyone who knows a campaign code and its fixed validOn timestamp can submit a forged couponData value and receive the corresponding discount, including the 75% campaign discount.

The discount calculation is invoked while constructing the order total.
If no stored basket coupon is present, the handler accepts req.body.couponData, decodes it from base64, and extracts the coupon code and date without a signature or server-issued token validation.
A caller-controlled code/date pair matching the static campaign table is accepted and its discount is returned.
The returned discount is applied directly to totalPrice, allowing the attacker to reduce the purchase price using forged campaign data.

title: Concurrent checkout requests can process one basket multiple times
description: Checkout processing is not atomic or idempotent. The handler reads the basket, decrements inventory, performs wallet operations, inserts an order, and only clears basket items asynchronously after PDF generation completes. Multiple concurrent requests for the same basket can all pass the initial lookup and process the same items before the deletion occurs, creating duplicate orders, repeated bonus credits or wallet races, and inventory decrements beyond the purchased quantity.

Each request independently reads the same basket and its included products before any checkout lock or state transition is applied.
Each concurrent request decrements inventory for the basket items without a transaction or conditional stock check.
Each request can independently debit the wallet and add bonus points based on the same basket.
Each request inserts an order before the basket items are destroyed; destruction occurs only later in the PDF writer finish callback, so parallel requests can all create orders for the same basket.

title: User-controlled username reaches server-side eval
description: An authenticated user's stored username is treated as executable JavaScript. If the username matches the `#{...}` pattern and the username-XSS challenge is enabled, the contents are extracted and passed directly to `eval()`. An attacker who can create or modify a username can therefore execute arbitrary server-side JavaScript in the application process, potentially reading secrets, accessing files, or compromising the server.

The handler uses the authenticated session's user ID to load the corresponding user record. The username subsequently used below is persisted user data and may originate from caller-controlled profile input elsewhere in the application.
The loaded username is explicitly recognized as an expression-bearing value when it matches `#{...}` and the challenge is enabled; the expression contents are extracted into `code`.
The extracted username contents are passed directly to JavaScript `eval()` without an allow-list or safe expression parser, creating a server-side code execution sink.

title: Persisted username injected into dynamically compiled Pug template
description: The handler substitutes the persisted username directly into the source text of a Pug template and then compiles that resulting text. This is template injection: a username containing Pug syntax or a newline can alter the template structure and may cause expressions or template code to execute when the compiled function is rendered. The preceding backslash is not a complete context-safe encoding of arbitrary template source.

trace.description: The exported profile handler receives the attacker-facing request; route registration and the caller are outside this file.
The handler loads the authenticated user's persisted record, including the username that will be inserted into the template.

The username is inserted into the raw Pug template source through string replacement. This is source-level substitution rather than escaped data rendering; the fallback only prepends a backslash and does not safely encode all template syntax or line boundaries.
The modified template string is passed to `pug.compile`, which interprets the attacker-influenced content as Pug template code before rendering it.

title: Hardcoded reusable passwords and TOTP secrets in authentication tests
description: The test source contains reusable authentication credentials, including a hardcoded password and TOTP secret for the seeded `wurstbrot` account (lines 139-143), as well as additional hardcoded 2FA enrollment secrets throughout the file. If these fixtures or accounts are available in a shared, staging, or accidentally production-like environment, anyone with repository access can generate valid TOTP codes and authenticate as the account. The secret material should be injected through isolated test configuration and test accounts should not use credentials that can be reused outside the test environment.

The hardcoded TOTP secret is passed to the login helper and used to obtain an authenticated token, making the secret reusable by anyone who can access the source or a corresponding seeded environment. Similar hardcoded secrets are also present at lines 182, 214, 240, 266, 292, and 352.

description: The test source contains a plaintext username and password used to authenticate as `jim@juice-sh.op`. Anyone with access to the repository can recover these credentials, and they could enable unauthorized access if the seeded account or password is available in a deployed or shared environment. Although this appears intended as a test fixture credential, it is still a hardcoded credential and should be isolated to disposable test data or injected through test-only secret configuration.

The setup hook creates the test application and then calls the authentication helper with a fixed account.
The authentication call receives the hardcoded email and plaintext password values from source-controlled test code.

title: Unbounded attacker-controlled code-fix cache enables memory exhaustion
description: The unauthenticated snippet-fix routes accept an attacker-controlled `key`. On every cache miss, `readFixes` scans the directory and then stores the result in the process-global `CodeFixes` object under that arbitrary key. An attacker can send requests with an unbounded sequence of unique keys, causing repeated synchronous directory scans and unbounded growth of the in-memory cache. Because the routes have no rate limit shown and are publicly reachable, this can consume CPU and memory until the service becomes degraded or unavailable.

The route parameter is copied directly into `key` and passed to `readFixes` without a length, format, or cardinality restriction.
Each cache miss performs a synchronous directory listing and file scan, so every novel attacker-supplied key triggers filesystem work.
The result is stored globally under the attacker-controlled key and is never evicted or bounded; repeated unique keys therefore grow `CodeFixes` without limit.

title: Path traversal in code-fix YAML metadata loader
description: The POST handler constructs a filesystem path using the unvalidated request-body `key`. Although the suffix is fixed to `.info.yml`, traversal sequences in `key` can escape `data/static/codefixes` and cause the server to read and parse attacker-selected files whose names end in that suffix. The parsed data can influence the returned explanation, and parsing arbitrary local YAML also exposes the endpoint to resource-intensive parsing of any reachable large YAML file. The path should be constrained to a strict challenge-key allow-list or resolved and verified to remain inside the intended directory.

The request body controls `key` at runtime; the TypeScript `ChallengeKey` annotation does not validate the incoming value.
The untrusted key is concatenated into a filesystem path without normalization, traversal rejection, or containment checking.
The resulting path is read and passed to `yaml.load`, allowing traversal to arbitrary reachable `*.info.yml` files and potentially expensive YAML parsing of attacker-selected local files.

title: Unauthenticated challenge completion state change
description: The unauthenticated POST /snippets/verdict endpoint can invoke the state-changing challenge completion operation for any valid challenge key. The route is registered with no authentication middleware, and the handler never derives or checks a user identity before calling solveFindIt. An unauthenticated caller can submit the required vulnerable line numbers and mark challenges as solved, potentially altering shared application progress or completing functionality intended for an authenticated user.

The caller also supplies selectedLines, which is checked only for correctness against the challenge's known vulnerable and neutral lines; there is no authentication or authorization check.
When the supplied verdict is true, the handler invokes solveFindIt(key), performing the challenge completion state change without any user or role check.

title: Unbounded selected-lines processing enables resource exhaustion
description: The unauthenticated verdict endpoint accepts an arbitrarily long selectedLines array and processes every element through repeated linear includes checks. getVerdict first checks every vulnerable line against the attacker-controlled array and then scans the entire array while checking membership in the combined vulnerable and neutral line lists. With a large request body, or many repeated requests because the route has no shown throttling, an attacker can consume disproportionate CPU and application memory. The handler also performs filesystem stat/read operations for each request.

The computation scans the complete attacker-controlled selectedLines array and performs another linear includes lookup for each element, allowing excessive CPU work for oversized input.

title: Hardcoded plaintext account credentials in test source
description: The test setup embeds a plaintext password for the `jim@juice-sh.op` account directly in the repository and passes it to the authentication helper. title: Basket ownership/state invariant bypass via initially omitted BasketId
description: The tests demonstrate an inconsistent basket-item state transition: a basket item can first be created without a `BasketId`, and then an authenticated caller can assign `BasketId: 3` in a later update, which returns 200. The neighboring tests establish that changing an existing item's basket is normally forbidden, so omitting the association at creation bypasses that invariant. If the selected basket belongs to another user, this permits moving or injecting an item into another user's basket; the ownership relationship for basket 3 cannot be confirmed from this file, so the access-control aspect is conditional on the route's missing ownership check.

title: Plaintext credentials hardcoded in test source
description: The test source contains plaintext authentication credentials embedded directly in calls to `login()`. The credentials are then sent as part of an authentication request, making them recoverable by anyone with repository access and potentially reusable against the corresponding accounts or environments. One credential appears to be a real-looking account password rather than a generated test-only secret.

title: Unauthenticated fixed-port mock server has unbounded request-body buffering
description: The fixed-port mock LLM server accepts network connections without authentication and accumulates the entire request body in memory with no size limit. A client able to reach port 43210 can keep sending data or submit an arbitrarily large body, causing unbounded memory growth and potentially exhausting the test process. This is primarily a test-environment exposure, but becomes a practical denial-of-service risk if the test process is reachable from an untrusted network.

title: Continue-code application accepts codes for nonexistent challenges

title: Authenticated users can read baskets by arbitrary ID
description: An authenticated caller can request another user's basket by substituting an arbitrary basket identifier. The test logs in as the Bjoern account, requests `/rest/basket/2`, and expects a successful response containing basket data. No ownership failure is expected or asserted, demonstrating object-level authorization is not enforced on this resource endpoint. An attacker with any valid account can enumerate basket IDs and read other users' basket contents.

The caller supplies the target object identifier directly in the URL as `/rest/basket/2` and attaches only a bearer token; the request does not provide any ownership proof.
The endpoint returns HTTP 200 and exposes the requested basket's ID, showing that authentication succeeds without a per-basket ownership check.

title: Basket coupon application and checkout lack object-level authorization
description: Basket mutation and checkout operations accept a caller-selected basket ID. The authenticated request applies a 99% discount to basket 2 and then successfully checks it out, with the test explicitly naming the coupon forged and asserting both the discount and successful order creation. This permits a caller to target a basket outside their ownership and obtain an unauthorized economic benefit or trigger an unauthorized purchase.

The caller-controlled forged coupon is placed in the URL while the authenticated session is supplied via `authHeader`.
The server accepts the coupon and reports a 99% discount for the selected basket, demonstrating that the caller can alter pricing state for the chosen basket.
The caller then checks out the same selected basket and receives an order confirmation, showing that the workflow permits completion after the unauthorized pricing mutation.

title: Hardcoded weak administrator credential
description: The test contains a hardcoded administrative login password (`admin123`) and uses it to authenticate to the application. If the seeded or deployed administrative account retains this credential, anyone who discovers the source or test environment can obtain administrative access. Even if intended only for tests, retaining a weak default administrator credential creates a dangerous configuration assumption.

The administrator password is hardcoded as the weak value `admin123` and is used to obtain a bearer token.
The resulting administrator token is attached to basket-item mutation and checkout requests, confirming the credential grants access to privileged application operations.

title: Internal exception details are returned in error responses
description: Error responses expose internal exception messages to the HTTP client. The tests deliberately inject failures from quantity lookup, wallet lookup, and order insertion, then assert that the response body contains the internal messages (`Quantity error`, `Wallet error`, and `Insert error`). In production, equivalent unhandled exception text can reveal implementation details and aid targeted attacks.

The test verifies that the raw internal exception text is present in the HTTP response body rather than replaced by a generic error.

title: Plaintext hardcoded authentication credentials in test source
description: The test source hardcodes plaintext credentials for two accounts, including the apparent CISO/deluxe account, and uses them to obtain bearer tokens. If these fixtures or accounts are reused in a deployed or shared environment, anyone with repository or artifact access can authenticate as those users; the privileged account could enable elevated access. The credentials should be injected through isolated test configuration or generated dynamically and must not be valid outside the test environment.

The deluxe/CISO test contains a second plaintext password for the ciso account, which appears more privileged and is used to obtain an authentication token.

title: Hardcoded and weak privileged account credentials in test source
description: The test source contains hardcoded account credentials, including the administrator password `admin123` and multiple customer/staff passwords. These values are passed directly to the shared `login` helper and therefore become usable authentication secrets wherever the seeded accounts are reachable. Anyone who can read the repository can obtain credentials for privileged or authenticated accounts; reuse of these fixtures outside an isolated test environment could enable unauthorized access. The administrator credential is also weak and default-like.

title: CAPTCHA answer exposed to clients, allowing CAPTCHA bypass
description: The data-export CAPTCHA is defeated because the test obtains the correct CAPTCHA answer directly from the `/rest/image-captcha` response (`captchaRes.body.answer`) and submits it to the export endpoint. Any authenticated client can follow the same flow, so the CAPTCHA does not provide meaningful anti-automation protection for data exports. This may enable automated export abuse if other throttling controls are absent.

The response is treated as containing the CAPTCHA solution in a client-readable `answer` field.
The client sends that response-derived answer to `/rest/user/data-export`, demonstrating that the CAPTCHA can be solved without user interaction or image recognition.
The export succeeds with the exposed answer, confirming the answer is accepted as the CAPTCHA credential.

title: Hardcoded weak administrative credentials in source
description: The test source contains hardcoded authentication credentials, including the administrative password `admin123` and several ordinary user passwords. If these accounts or equivalent seeded credentials are available outside an isolated test database, disclosure of the repository permits direct authentication; `admin123` is also a weak default-style administrative credential. The administrative credential is passed directly into the login helper.

The test constructs the administrative account identity and invokes the authentication helper with a literal password.
The hardcoded `admin123` credential reaches the login operation, creating a reusable source-level administrative credential if the seeded account is reachable in a deployed or shared environment.

title: Authenticated arbitrary file read through unvalidated erasure layout path
description: The authenticated POST /dataerasure/ flow accepts the caller-controlled `layout` value as a filesystem-relative path and returns content from an existing file outside the intended erasure-form resource. Supplying `../package.json` succeeds and the response contains `juice-shop`, demonstrating arbitrary local file read/path traversal. Any authenticated user who can reach this endpoint may read other files accessible to the server process by substituting paths such as configuration files, source files, or environment-related files. The server must derive the layout from an allowlisted value or constrain resolution to the intended directory rather than trusting the request field.

trace.description: The test exercises the attacker-facing POST `/dataerasure/` endpoint using an authenticated session; the route handler itself is outside this file.
The request supplies `layout` as `../package.json`, allowing the caller to select a filesystem path rather than an approved form layout.
The application returns HTTP 200 and response content containing `juice-shop`, confirming that the selected file was read and its contents were exposed to the requester.
The response is further asserted to contain recognizable file content, establishing that this is file disclosure rather than merely path validation or a rendered default template.

title: Raw filesystem errors exposed by erasure layout endpoint
description: The same unauthenticated-facing error path returns a 500 response containing an internal filesystem error (`no such file or directory`) when a caller supplies a nonexistent layout path. This exposes backend implementation details and confirms that attacker-controlled filesystem operations are allowed to surface raw operational errors through the HTTP response, aiding path probing and reconnaissance. Errors should be handled with a generic client response while details are recorded in protected server logs.

trace.description: The test sends an authenticated POST request to `/dataerasure/`; the route implementation and its error handling are outside this file.
The caller controls the `layout` path and supplies a deliberately nonexistent traversal path.
The endpoint returns HTTP 500 and the response body contains the raw filesystem error text `no such file or directory`, exposing internal operation details to the requester.
The test explicitly verifies that the error text is present in the HTTP response rather than being suppressed behind a generic error message.

title: Unauthenticated directory listing of encryption keys
description: The application exposes the `/encryptionkeys` directory without any authentication or authorization. The test expects a successful HTML directory listing, allowing an unauthenticated caller to enumerate encryption-related files and discover sensitive key material. This is a dangerous static-file configuration and can facilitate further compromise of protected content.

The request is sent directly through the Express test application with no credentials, authorization header, or ownership check.
The test requires HTTP 200 and HTML containing `listing directory /encryptionkeys`, establishing that the directory listing is intentionally exposed to unauthenticated callers.

title: Public exposure of the premium-content AES key
description: A sensitive AES key used for premium content is directly retrievable from `/encryptionkeys/premium.key` without authentication. Any network caller can obtain the key and potentially decrypt or reproduce access to content that the application intends to protect. The test confirms a successful 200 response and contains no compensating access control.

trace.description: The test performs an unauthenticated GET request for `/encryptionkeys/premium.key`; the serving route is implemented outside this file.
The key path is supplied directly to the application request and no session, role, or other authorization material is provided.
The test asserts a successful 200 response for the AES key file, demonstrating that the cryptographic key is publicly retrievable.

title: Unauthenticated exposure of access log files
description: The application serves an access log file through a public URL constructed from the current timestamp. The test makes the request without authentication and expects a successful octet-stream response. Exposing access logs can disclose request paths, identifiers, timestamps, client information, and other operational data, impairing monitoring confidentiality and potentially aiding attacks.

trace.description: The test exercises a GET request for `/support/logs/access.log.<timestamp>`; the actual static-file route and its caller are outside this file.
The requested log filename is assembled from the current time and sent through the application without credentials or authorization checks.
The test requires HTTP 200 and `application/octet-stream`, confirming that an access log is served to the unauthenticated requester.

title: Feedback creation allows arbitrary user attribution
description: The feedback creation API accepts a caller-supplied `UserId` and persists it without enforcing that it matches the authenticated user or otherwise checking authorization. The test demonstrates both anonymous attribution to UserId 3 and authenticated attribution to a different UserId, with the server returning 201 and the requested owner ID. An attacker can therefore create feedback impersonating another user or corrupt ownership/audit data.

trace.description: The caller outside this test file reaches `POST /api/Feedbacks`; this test invokes the attacker-facing endpoint as an anonymous user.
The request body includes attacker-controlled `UserId: 3` together with otherwise valid feedback and CAPTCHA data.
The endpoint accepts the request and returns HTTP 201, showing that an unauthenticated caller can create feedback attributed to the supplied user ID.
The same endpoint is invoked with an authenticated token while supplying a different arbitrary `UserId: 3`; the caller's identity is not used to constrain the submitted owner.
The successful response preserves the arbitrary supplied `UserId`, confirming unauthorized attribution and integrity corruption.

title: Hardcoded reusable login credential in test source
description: A reusable account password is hardcoded in the test source and passed directly to the login helper. The value is merely Base64-encoded, which is reversible and provides no secrecy. Anyone who obtains the repository or test artifacts can reuse the credential against the test environment, and potentially against other environments if the account or password was reused.

The login input contains a hardcoded password string in source code.
The hardcoded credential is passed to `login`, where it is used for authentication rather than being obtained from a secret store or isolated test fixture.

title: Server accepts executable uploads rejected by client validation
description: The test demonstrates that the attacker-facing POST /file-upload endpoint accepts an executable file and returns success, despite the file being identified as illegal by client-side validation. The server therefore appears to trust or omit the file-type restriction that the client is expected to enforce. An attacker can submit an executable directly to the API, bypassing client validation. The impact depends on how uploaded files are stored or later served, but could include arbitrary file hosting, stored content attacks, or unsafe downstream processing.

trace.description: The test sends an attacker-controlled upload request to POST /file-upload; the route implementation is outside this file.
The request attaches a file named invalidTypeForClient.exe, demonstrating that the uploaded content can have an executable type and that the API is tested independently of client-side validation.
The test expects HTTP 204, confirming that the server accepts the executable upload rather than rejecting it with a server-side type-validation error.

title: Plaintext account password hardcoded in test source
description: The test source contains a plaintext password for the `jim` account and submits it to the login helper. If this account or password is shared with a deployed/test environment, or if repository contents are exposed, an attacker can authenticate as that user. Although it may be intended as a fixture credential, the file provides no indication that the credential is isolated, ephemeral, or injected from a secure secret store.

The login request is populated with the fixed account email and the plaintext password literal `ncc-1701`, rather than obtaining the credential from a protected secret or ephemeral fixture.
The hardcoded password is supplied as the credential for the authentication operation, allowing anyone who obtains the source and can reach the corresponding account to attempt login as `jim`.

title: Hardcoded privileged account credentials in test source
description: The test source contains plaintext credentials for privileged or otherwise seeded accounts, including the administrator password `admin123` at line 76 and the support-team password at line 90, alongside additional reusable account passwords at lines 104, 118, 132, and 147. Anyone with access to the repository, published source bundle, or leaked test artifacts can use these credentials against an environment where the corresponding accounts exist. The administrator credential is also weak and predictable.

The test submits a hardcoded administrator email and password to the login endpoint.
The administrator password is explicitly hardcoded as `admin123`, demonstrating a weak reusable credential rather than a secret supplied securely at runtime.
The test also submits a hardcoded support-team password to the same authentication endpoint, confirming that reusable privileged credentials are embedded in source.

title: Client-controlled login IP telemetry can be spoofed
description: The test demonstrates that an authenticated caller can provide an arbitrary `True-Client-IP` header and have that value accepted as the recorded last login IP. Unless a trusted reverse proxy strips or overwrites this header before the application, a user can forge login-location telemetry, undermining audit trails and any detection based on login IPs. The route implementation is outside this file, so proxy enforcement and downstream authorization cannot be confirmed here.

After authenticating, the test sends a caller-selected `true-client-ip` value of `1.2.3.4` in the request header.

The endpoint response is asserted to contain the exact caller-supplied IP, showing that the header value reaches the login-IP recording behavior without a visible trust or validation check in this trace.

title: Unauthenticated FTP directory listing exposes internal files
description: The FTP endpoint is reachable without authentication and returns a directory listing. An attacker can enumerate available files and identify sensitive backups, documents, and credential stores before requesting them. The test sends a bare GET request and expects HTTP 200 with a directory-listing title, demonstrating that the exposure is active.

The endpoint is expected to return HTTP 200 for the unauthenticated request.
The response is confirmed to contain a directory listing for /ftp, allowing resource enumeration.

title: Unauthenticated exposure of confidential FTP document
description: An unauthenticated request to /ftp/acquisitions.md returns HTTP 200 and contains the confidential Planned Acquisitions document. This exposes an internal resource directly through the FTP route to any attacker who knows or enumerates the filename.

The request is propagated to the confidential acquisitions document under the FTP route.
The application is expected to return HTTP 200 for the unauthenticated document request.

title: Unauthenticated exposure of KeePass credential database
description: An unauthenticated request to /ftp/incident-support.kdbx returns HTTP 200. A KeePass database is a credential-bearing internal resource; exposing it through a public file endpoint can enable compromise of accounts and connected systems.

title: Encoded-null filename bypass exposes FTP backup artifact
description: The FTP route exposes a backup package.json file through a null-byte-encoded filename bypass. The direct .bak suffix is rejected elsewhere, but /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md returns HTTP 200 and reveals dependency metadata. This demonstrates inconsistent extension validation and exposure of an internal backup artifact.

The response is buffered for retrieval as file content.
The application returns HTTP 200 for the bypass request, and the response contains package.json backup dependency data, confirming that the validation workflow can be bypassed.

title: Unauthenticated exposure of operational metrics endpoint
description: The test explicitly verifies that an unauthenticated client can request GET /metrics and receive HTTP 200 text containing operational metrics, including application version, registered-user counts, request counters, challenge progress, and cheat-score data. If this test app configuration reflects the deployed route, the metrics endpoint is publicly exposed without authentication, allowing reconnaissance and disclosure of internal operational information. The production reachability and intended exposure policy cannot be confirmed from this file alone.

The test setup initializes and wires the metrics route onto the test application without showing any authentication or authorization middleware around it.
The request is expected to return HTTP 200 and text/plain content directly, demonstrating that an unauthenticated caller can retrieve the metrics response.

title: Hardcoded reusable credentials for privileged test accounts
description: The test source embeds reusable account credentials for administrator, customer, and accountant accounts (for example, `admin123` and `i am an awesome accountant`) and submits them to the authentication helper. If this test fixture or its seeded credentials are exposed or reused in a reachable environment, an attacker can authenticate as these users, including privileged roles. The issue is somewhat context-dependent because the file is under `test/` and the accounts may be intentionally isolated test fixtures, but hardcoded credentials should not be reused outside a controlled test environment.

description: The test source contains a plaintext username and password used to obtain an authenticated bearer token. Anyone with access to the repository can recover these credentials and attempt authentication against any environment where the test account exists, potentially gaining access as that user. Storing reusable credentials in source is a security misconfiguration, even if the account is intended only for testing; the risk is higher if test credentials are shared with staging or production data.

title: Unauthenticated product update due to missing function-level access control
description: The product update endpoint accepts an unauthenticated PUT request and successfully modifies an existing product. The test explicitly sends no Authorization header, supplies a product identifier, and observes a 200 response with the attacker-controlled description persisted. Any unauthenticated caller can therefore tamper with product data, potentially affecting application integrity and downstream rendering.

The API returns HTTP 200 and the response contains the supplied description, demonstrating that the unauthenticated mutation succeeds.

title: Plaintext passwords transmitted in password-change URL query parameters
description: The password-change endpoint is exercised with the current password and replacement passwords embedded in the URL query string, for example at line 35. URLs are commonly captured by reverse proxies, web servers, browser history, analytics, monitoring systems, and referrer headers, so plaintext credentials can persist outside the request body and be disclosed to operators or downstream systems. This is an unsafe authentication workflow design even when transport encryption is enabled.

The request places `current`, `new`, and `repeat` password values directly in the query string, including the current password and replacement password.

The request is sent with only an Authorization header while the credentials remain in the URL, allowing intermediary access logging, browser history, proxy logs, and related URL-recording mechanisms to capture the plaintext passwords.

title: Hardcoded account passwords and security answers in test source
description: This test source contains multiple plaintext authentication credentials and security-question answers for named accounts, including passwords at lines 44, 95, 128, 142, 156, and 170 and answers at lines 113, 127, 141, 155, and 169. Anyone who can read the repository or a distributed source artifact can use these values against the corresponding seeded or deployed accounts if they remain valid. Test credentials may be intentionally isolated, so exploitability outside test environments depends on deployment and account reuse, but the credentials are nevertheless hardcoded in source.

description: The test source contains a reusable account credential: the literal email `bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com` and the password `bW9jLmxpYW1nQGhjaW5pbW1pay5ucmVvamI=` are passed directly to `login` at lines 93-95, and the same credential is duplicated at lines 107-109. These credentials are committed to the repository and may be copied into other environments, reused outside the test harness, or exposed through source/package distribution. title: Profile image URL upload permits server-side requests to localhost and internal services
description: The profile-image URL endpoint accepts a caller-supplied URL and server-side processing reaches an attacker-controlled localhost service. The test starts a local HTTP server, submits its localhost URL in the `imageUrl` field, and expects the request to succeed and the image to be processed. An authenticated attacker could substitute loopback, private-network, cloud-metadata, or internal-service URLs to make the application initiate requests from its own network position, enabling SSRF and potentially internal data or administrative access.

title: Unauthenticated redirect errors expose Express and TypeError implementation details
description: The attacker-facing GET /redirect endpoint returns a 500 HTML response containing the application name, Express error context, a TypeError, and implementation-specific text such as "of undefined" and "includes" when the required query parameter is absent. This exposes stack/error details to unauthenticated callers, assisting endpoint probing and vulnerability exploitation. The test explicitly verifies that this information leakage occurs; the vulnerable error handling is implemented outside this test file.

The route responds with HTTP 500 and an HTML error page, rather than a controlled client error response.

The response body is asserted to contain the application name, Express marker, TypeError, undefined-property text, and the internal method name 'includes', demonstrating unauthenticated exposure of diagnostic implementation details.

title: Unauthenticated security-question lookup enables account enumeration
description: The unauthenticated `/rest/user/security-question` endpoint reveals whether an email address belongs to an account and, for recognized addresses, returns that account's security question. An attacker can submit candidate email addresses and distinguish existing users from unknown users based on the response body (`question` versus `{}`). Exposing the security-question prompt also assists attacks against a weak knowledge-based account-recovery mechanism.

The request accepts an attacker-supplied `email` query parameter and sends it without authentication or an authorization header.
For a recognized email, the response is successful and contains the user's security-question text.
A second request supplies an unknown email address, providing the comparison case needed for enumeration.
The endpoint returns an empty object for the unknown address, so an attacker can distinguish registered addresses from unregistered ones and obtain security-question prompts for registered accounts.

title: Missing email causes verbose internal error disclosure
description: The endpoint returns HTTP 500 and an HTML error response when the required `email` parameter is omitted. The test explicitly requires the response to contain the application name and a detailed database/ORM error (`WHERE parameter "email" has invalid "undefined" value`). This indicates verbose production-style error disclosure, which can reveal implementation details and should instead be handled as a controlled client error without internal diagnostics.

The response body exposes the application name and a raw ORM/database WHERE-clause error, disclosing internal implementation details to the caller.

title: Authenticated caller can create a security answer for a caller-supplied user ID
description: The test creates a new user, then submits a security answer for that user's identifier while using an authorization token created before the user registration. The request body controls `UserId` (line 70), and the endpoint returns 201 (line 75), with no evidence in this file that the authenticated principal is checked against the target user. An authenticated attacker could substitute another user's ID—particularly an account without an existing security answer—and set or claim its security answer, potentially corrupting account-recovery state or enabling recovery abuse.

The request is authenticated with the shared `authHeader`, whose token was generated before the newly registered user was created; this establishes that the request principal is not derived from the target user created in the test.
The target account is selected through the caller-controlled `UserId` body field rather than being derived from the authenticated identity.
The application accepts the cross-identity security-answer creation and returns HTTP 201, demonstrating successful mutation without a visible per-user ownership check in this test path.

title: Unauthenticated registration permits self-assignment of the admin role
description: The public user-registration endpoint accepts a caller-supplied `role` property and creates the account with that role. The request does not include authentication, yet submitting `role: 'admin'` returns HTTP 201 and the response confirms the created user has the admin role. An attacker can therefore self-register an administrative account by adding the role field to the registration request.

The externally supplied request body includes the sensitive privilege-bearing property `role: 'admin'` alongside the normal registration fields.
The endpoint returns 201 and the response contains `role: 'admin'`, demonstrating that the caller-controlled role was accepted and persisted rather than restricted to a server-selected default.

title: User-controlled fields parameter exposes password data
description: The `/rest/user/whoami` endpoint allows the caller to select response fields through the `fields` query parameter, including the sensitive `password` property. The test confirms that an authenticated user can request `fields=id,email,password` and receive a password string. Exposing password material enables offline password cracking and violates property-level authorization for sensitive account data.

The response is asserted to contain a string-valued `user.password`, showing that the caller-controlled field selection reaches the returned user properties without a sensitive-field exclusion.

title: Configuration validator accepts cleartext system-wide notification endpoints
description: The configuration validation contract explicitly treats an `http://` system-wide notification URL as valid. If this feature is configured to contact a non-local endpoint, notification traffic can be observed or modified in transit, allowing disclosure or tampering with notification data. The production caller and transport behavior are outside this file, so the severity depends on what data the notification client sends and whether HTTPS is enforced elsewhere.

The test asserts that the validator accepts the cleartext endpoint as valid, demonstrating that this validation path does not require HTTPS or otherwise reject non-secure notification transport.

title: MD5 used for authentication-related hashing
description: The exported `security.hash` operation is explicitly specified and tested as MD5 for arbitrary input, including common passwords. MD5 is unsuitable for password storage or authentication-related hashing because it is fast, unsalted, and vulnerable to efficient offline dictionary and rainbow-table attacks. If hashes produced by this helper protect credentials or authentication decisions, an attacker who obtains them can recover weak passwords and take over accounts.

The test confirms that the function returns the known MD5 digest for `admin123`, demonstrating that the hashing operation uses MD5 rather than a password-strengthening construction such as Argon2, scrypt, or bcrypt.

title: Predictable and forgeable discount coupons
description: Coupon values are deterministically derived from the discount and month/year and are directly reversible with Base85. The tests show that the encoded payload contains values such as `JAN80-20`, that the same inputs always produce the same coupon, and that a valid coupon can represent a discount of 99. Because no unpredictable secret, signature, or server-side issuance state is evidenced, an attacker who knows the format can construct a current-period coupon for an arbitrary permitted discount and submit it for redemption.

The generated value is decoded directly into a plaintext month/year and discount payload (`JAN80-20`), showing that the coupon carries predictable business data rather than an opaque, authenticated token.
The tests establish deterministic generation for the same month and discount and show that day and time do not add entropy, making the space of valid current coupons readily enumerable.
A coupon generated for a 99% discount is accepted by `discountFromCoupon`; an attacker can reproduce the same construction for a target discount and redeem it.

title: Caller-controlled user identity from x-user-email header
description: `security.userEmailFrom` accepts the `x-user-email` request header as the user's email without any visible authentication or integrity check. Since request headers are caller-controlled, an attacker can claim another user's email wherever downstream code relies on this helper for identity, potentially causing unauthorized access or actions as that user. The exact downstream authorization use is outside this file, so exploitability depends on callers treating this value as trusted identity.

The test confirms that an arbitrary caller-supplied `x-user-email` value is returned verbatim, with no token validation, session lookup, signature verification, or other identity binding visible at this boundary.

title: ERC20 approve allows allowance front-running race
description: The allowance-update design permits the well-known ERC20 approval race. A token holder can call approve() to replace an existing nonzero allowance, while the authorized spender can observe and front-run that transaction by calling transferFrom() against the old allowance. After the approval succeeds, the spender can also use the new allowance, potentially spending both values. The contract provides increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance, but does not prevent unsafe direct replacement through approve().

The supplied spender and amount are forwarded directly to _approve without requiring the current allowance to be zero or otherwise preventing replacement of a nonzero allowance.
_approve overwrites the existing allowance in one operation. A spender can front-run the overwrite using transferFrom against the old allowance and then spend the newly assigned allowance.

title: Unbounded privileged minting enables arbitrary token inflation
description: The contract exposes an owner-controlled mint operation with no maximum supply, per-recipient limit, or other issuance constraint. Although onlyOwner prevents arbitrary callers from invoking it, the deployer can mint an unlimited number of tokens to any recipient, increasing totalSupply and diluting existing holders. If the declared initial supply is intended to represent a fixed or bounded issuance, this is an exploitable economic design flaw by the privileged owner or any compromise of the owner key.

The only authorization check is onlyOwner, which permits the single stored owner to invoke issuance but imposes no supply cap, rate limit, or issuance policy.
The requested amount is passed directly to _mint, which increases total supply and the recipient balance by that amount.
_mint performs unbounded arithmetic addition to _totalSupply and the recipient balance, then emits a normal mint Transfer event; repeated calls can create arbitrary token supply and dilute holders.

title: Unauthenticated chat can mint arbitrary discount coupons
description: The public POST /rest/chat route exposes an LLM tool that generates discount coupons, but the tool performs no authentication, order verification, damage verification, prior return/exchange rejection, or server-side discount bound check. The policy exists only in the system prompt and is not an authorization control. An unauthenticated caller can submit messages that induce the model to call generateCoupon with an arbitrary numeric discount, and the tool directly passes that value to security.generateCoupon. This can mint unauthorized or excessive-value coupons.

The handler accepts caller-supplied messages and gives them to the LLM together with the generateCoupon tool.
The model is allowed to invoke generateCoupon; the surrounding coupon conditions are only natural-language system-prompt instructions, not server-enforced checks.

The generateCoupon tool accepts any Zod-valid number and immediately calls security.generateCoupon without checking authentication, ownership of a damaged order, return rejection, or a maximum discount.

title: User-controlled username is injected into the LLM system prompt
description: A database-backed username is interpolated directly into the system prompt as instruction-like text without fencing or neutralization. A user who can control their username can place prompt-injection content into the system-level context, potentially overriding chatbot policies and influencing tool use. In this file, the affected model has access to a coupon-generation tool whose authorization is not independently enforced, increasing the impact beyond merely changing response wording.

The resulting string is supplied as the model's system instruction, allowing injected username text to be interpreted as higher-priority instructions and potentially alter tool behavior.

title: Unauthenticated chat accepts unbounded input and has no visible throttling
description: POST /rest/chat is publicly reachable and accepts req.body.messages without a message-count, content-length, token, or total conversation-size limit. The handler starts an LLM stream for every request, and the configured step cap only limits agent steps; it does not bound the initial input or request frequency. An attacker can send very large message histories or repeatedly invoke the endpoint to consume LLM tokens, memory, connection slots, and upstream API capacity. Deployment-level limits may mitigate this, but no application-level control is present in this file.

The handler exposes an LLM streaming operation without a per-user/IP rate limit, request-size limit, or input-token limit; the stepCountIs(10) setting limits tool steps but not input consumption.

title: Unauthenticated User registration uses unrestricted model property binding
description: The generated User REST resource accepts caller-supplied properties without an explicit allow-list. The registration endpoint is reachable without authentication and only excludes `password` and `totpSecret`; all other model properties are implicitly bindable by finale-rest. An attacker can submit fields that should be server-controlled, such as authorization, verification, or account-state properties exposed by the User model, potentially causing privilege escalation or bypassing account-state checks.

title: Any authenticated user can create products through the generated API
description: The Product collection's POST endpoint is protected only by `security.isAuthorized()`, which establishes authentication but not an administrative or role-specific permission. The subsequent generated finale-rest resource exposes POST handling for `/api/Products` with no deny-all or admin middleware. Any authenticated user can create Product records, potentially altering catalog integrity, prices, or other product metadata.

title: Generated collection endpoints return unbounded result sets
description: All generated REST resources explicitly disable pagination. The unauthenticated Product GET collection is not protected by authorization middleware, so an attacker can repeatedly request the entire product table. As the table grows, each request can force an unbounded database read, object materialization, and response serialization, creating a denial-of-service and memory/bandwidth risk.

title: Hardcoded cookie-signing secret
description: The application configures cookie-parser with the hardcoded signing secret `kekse`. Anyone who obtains this source or a deployed copy can forge valid signed cookies, and the secret cannot be rotated independently of the application artifact. Any security-sensitive signed cookie used by this application can consequently be modified or fabricated.

title: Development error handler exposed in the running server
description: The production application always installs the `errorhandler` development middleware. On unhandled errors, this middleware can return detailed stack traces and internal error information to remote clients. Attackers can trigger malformed requests or other errors and use the responses to disclose filesystem paths, module details, and implementation data useful for further attacks.

title: Unauthenticated FTP directory listing and file download
description: The server publicly enables directory browsing for `/ftp` and serves files below that path without an authentication middleware. Directory indexes disclose filenames and attackers can request files directly, exposing any sensitive, temporary, backup, or challenge-related content placed in the FTP directory.
